From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from our playbook, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel — Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**To:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Re:** Departures from Buyer Playbook and recommended pushback

## 1. Threshold point: the "FINAL / settled at principal level" framing

Before the substantive clauses, note the Seller's preamble: it asserts that the enclosed positions "were settled at principal level by both deal teams" and are "marked FINAL and not intended to be re-opened."

**This should be rejected outright.** Our playbook records no authority from Amelia Frost for any of the fallback positions (20% cap, 18-month period), and no record of principal-level agreement on any of these terms. The preamble is a negotiation anchor dressed as a factual statement of agreement. It also tries to pre-load the reviewer with "market standard" ranges (10–20% cap, 1% basket, 12–18 months, knowledge qualifiers) that happen to coincide with the Seller's draft. We should not treat any of this as binding, agreed, or as evidence of market. Respond that nothing is agreed until documented in the SPA, and ask the Seller to identify any written record of the supposed principal-level agreement — there will be none.

Note also the internal tension in the Seller's own pack: the Disclosure Letter at [11] expressly says "No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included." The cover note's claim of a "settled" bargain contradicts the Seller's own disclosure document.

---

## 2. Clause-by-clause departures

### 2.1 Clause 12.1 — General warranty cap: 20% / AUD 4.8m
**Playbook:** 25% / AUD 6,000,000 opening position. 20% is a fallback usable **only** with prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft. None given.
**Departure:** Yes. The Seller has opened at our fallback and labelled it final.
**Pushback:** Counter at 25% / AUD 6.0m. Do not signal that 20% is acceptable. If the deal team wants to move, that is an Amelia Frost decision, documented in writing by reference to this draft (SPA-003 / Seller Update).

### 2.2 Clause 12.2 — De minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000; excess-only recovery
**Playbook:** De minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; **first-dollar (tipping) basket** once exceeded.
**Departure:** Material on all three elements:
- De minimis is 5x our position.
- Basket is 5x our position (and the Seller's "1% of price" framing = AUD 240k, so even on their own stated benchmark they are above it).
- The basket is a deductible, not a tipping basket. On a AUD 250k deductible, the first AUD 250k of loss is simply gone.
**Pushback:** Revert to AUD 5k / AUD 50k / first-dollar recovery. The combination of a high deductible with a low cap is the most economically damaging part of the liability package and should be a priority.

### 2.3 Clause 12.3 / 13 — 18-month claims period; limitations apply to "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"
**Playbook:** 24 months. 18 months is a fallback requiring Amelia Frost written approval (none given). Fundamental/Title claims at least six years, in a separate regime.
**Departure:** Two separate problems:
1. 18 months is our unauthorised fallback.
2. The "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" default is a **hidden general-regime override**. It would sweep Title, Tax, IP, payment and covenant claims, and the specific indemnities (Ironquay), into the 18-month window and the 20% cap unless each is individually carved out. This is precisely what our playbook instructs us to prevent.
**Pushback:** 24 months for general claims. Delete the "all Claims unless expressly stated" default and replace it with the reverse: the general limitations apply **only** to general Warranty Claims; everything else sits under its own regime.

### 2.4 Fundamental / Title warranties subject to general caps and time limits
**Playbook:** Separate regime; 100% of price cap; at least six years; outside basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.
**Departure:** Fundamental. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap title to 100% of the shares at 20% of the price. If the Seller does not actually own the shares, a AUD 4.8m recovery on a AUD 24m purchase is not an acceptable outcome.
**Pushback:** Non-negotiable. Separate regime for Title and Capacity: 100% cap, ≥6 years, no de minimis/basket, no knowledge qualifier, no disclosure qualification.

### 2.5 Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 — Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature"
**Playbook:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive this.
**Departure:** The Seller's draft contains **no fraud carve-out at all**. "All Claims of any nature" would, on its face, cap and time-bar fraud claims and have the Buyer disclaim reliance on fraudulent statements. This is unlikely to be fully enforceable in NSW, but we should not rely on a court to fix the drafting, and the attempt itself tells us something about the Seller's approach.
**Pushback:** Insert an express fraud / wilful concealment / deliberate misconduct carve-out from every limitation, the exclusive remedy clause and the non-reliance clause. This is a walk-away item under the playbook and cannot be traded.

### 2.6 Schedule 7 and Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2] — Whole-data-room and public-register deemed disclosure
**Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure only. Reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.
**Departure:** [1.1] discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the entire data room; [1.2] adds the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records." Combined with Clause 8.3 (below), this would effectively qualify every warranty by everything in the data room and everything a search could have found.
**Pushback:** Delete [1.1] and [1.2] as general disclosures. Replace with a fair disclosure standard: disclosure must be specific, with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter disclosed. Data-room documents may be referenced only where specifically cross-referred against an identified warranty.

Note the Seller's reservation at [1.4] ("nothing in this letter admits ... that any consent, payment, notice ... is legally required") — this is standard, but we should ensure our specific indemnities and conditions do not depend on any Seller admission.

### 2.7 Clause 8.3 — Buyer knowledge exclusion, including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records"
**Playbook:** Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions. Any qualifier must reference named Seller knowledge persons plus reasonable enquiry. Never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.
**Departure:** This is a blanket exclusion, extended to advisers and to constructive knowledge ("discoverable from"). It would convert every piece of due diligence we did into a defence for the Seller, and would arguably bar claims on the very matters disclosed as open (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-006) because we "knew" about them.
**Pushback:** Delete Clause 8.3 entirely. If any knowledge concept survives, it goes the other way — Seller warranties qualified by the actual knowledge of named Seller individuals after reasonable enquiry — and it must never apply to Title, Capacity, fraud or the specific indemnities.

### 2.8 Clauses 3 / 6.3 — Bluefen consent: reasonable endeavours; satisfied on delivery of written consent
**Playbook:** Effective consent **and** evidence that the 11.3 conditions are satisfied, before Completion. Not consent-on-delivery. Reasonable endeavours is insufficient for a material customer consent.
**Departure:** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue. The Seller's own Disclosure Letter [2] confirms no final written consent and no evidence of condition satisfaction is in the data room. The draft would treat the condition as satisfied on mere delivery of a piece of paper, regardless of whether the 11.3 conditions attached to that consent have been met — i.e. a conditional consent that could later fail.
**Pushback:** Condition precedent in our favour: (a) unconditional written consent from Bluefen under cl. 11.2, or conditional consent with documentary evidence that every cl. 11.3 condition is satisfied, (b) delivered before Completion, (c) Seller obligation at "all reasonable endeavours" at minimum, with cooperation covenants and a Buyer right to approach Bluefen directly. Consider a specific indemnity or price adjustment if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces within a defined period post-Completion.

### 2.9 Clauses 2 / 7 — Riverlark: release "following Completion"
**Playbook:** Current payout letter; direct repayment from Completion funds; effective security releases at Completion. A post-completion release requires an irrevocable undertaking **and** Amelia Frost approval.
**Departure:** ~AUD 3.2m facility; Disclosure Letter [3] confirms not repaid and no discharge. The draft defers the release to an unspecified post-Completion date, with no undertaking, no payout figure, and no mechanism for repayment from the purchase price. Riverlark's change-of-control clause (8.1) means Completion itself may be an event of default. On a debt-free/cash-free deal, we would be buying a company with AUD 3.2m of secured debt and a bank entitled to accelerate.
**Pushback:** Completion deliverables to include: current Riverlark payout letter; irrevocable direction for repayment out of Completion funds; executed deeds of release / PPSR discharge (or the bank's irrevocable undertaking to release on receipt of funds, delivered in escrow). If the deal team is prepared to accept any post-Completion element, that needs an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark **and** written approval from Amelia Frost — neither exists.

### 2.10 Funds flow — DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420,000) "a matter for the Seller", not itemised
**Playbook:** AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or Seller-funded; the funds flow must not silently exclude them.
**Departure:** The Seller describes the bonuses as its matter but then leaves them out of the funds flow — which means the Company (post-Completion, i.e. us) will pay them. The Disclosure Letter [5] confirms the amounts are absent from the funds flow and is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs. The true cost is therefore more than AUD 420k.
**Pushback:** Either (a) express line item in the funds flow deducting the bonuses plus employer on-costs (superannuation, payroll tax, leave accruals triggered) from the price, or (b) Seller to fund them directly with evidence of payment at Completion and a specific indemnity for any shortfall. Ask the Seller now to confirm the on-cost position and gross figure. Treat these as Transaction Expenses / debt-like items in the completion mechanics.

### 2.11 Clause 11.1 — Ironquay IP: indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment
**Playbook:** Broaden the narrow indemnity while preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is not independently verified either way.
**Departure:** The Seller's draft indemnifies only the specific SOW3 payment. But the risk is not the AUD 180k — it is that under DD-004 cl. 7.3 the SOW3 Project Materials **do not transfer** until every SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds. The Disclosure Letter [4] confirms no receipt of payment and no confirmatory assignment is in the data room. If title to the deliverables has not passed, the Company may not own IP it is using, and the exposure includes third-party claims, licence replacement, product downtime, and loss of customer revenue — not merely AUD 180k.
**Pushback:** Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss arising from (i) any failure of the SOW3 Project Materials (or any other Ironquay deliverables) to have validly vested in the Company, and (ii) any Ironquay claim. Preserve the cure: Seller to procure payment of all outstanding SOW3 fees in cleared funds and a confirmatory assignment from Ironquay **before Completion**, as a Completion deliverable. Do not treat DD-010's AUD 180k as established — require a statement of account from Ironquay. The indemnity must sit outside the general cap, basket and time limit (see 2.3).

### 2.12 Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 — DD-006 export/privacy incident: "preliminary, not expected to be material"
**Playbook:** Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction.
**Departure:** The Seller's characterisation ("not expected to be material") goes further than its own evidence. The Disclosure Letter [6] correctly states the investigation is preliminary and that access, scope and notification are all undetermined. ~1,240 records with names, business emails, roles and timestamps may or may not reach the Privacy Act / OAIC notifiable data breach threshold; we don't know yet and neither does the Seller.
**Pushback:** Do not accept "not material" as a warranty qualification, and do not ourselves assert a breach or demand a number — the playbook is clear on that. Require: (a) covenant to preserve all logs, link-access records and correspondence; (b) completion of the investigation (or a defined status) before Completion with a written report; (c) ongoing update obligation; (d) a specific indemnity for loss arising from the incident, sitting outside the general regime, with no price number attached unless and until facts emerge; (e) disclosure of the DD-006 matter to be specific and not read as disclosing "any" privacy non-compliance generally.

### 2.13 Supplier renewals — Sandbar AUD 330,000 "ordinary course"
**Playbook:** Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.
**Departure:** Minor. The Seller's "ordinary course" label is a conclusion; the Disclosure Letter [8] admits the material does not say whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. We shouldn't accept the label but also shouldn't over-reach by treating them as Debt.
**Pushback:** Request the three renewal documents (DD-008 / DD-011) read together, with term, termination rights and whether any amount is already accrued or pre-paid. If any amount is accrued and unpaid at Completion, it belongs in Working Capital / Debt-like items under the completion accounts, on the merits — not by assertion.

### 2.14 Tax / IP — "settled under the general regime"
**Playbook:** Tax and IP terms remain OPEN; separate categories; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution.
**Departure:** The Seller is attempting to close Tax and IP by folding them into the 20%/18-month general regime via the Clause 13 default. Nothing has been agreed.
**Pushback:** State expressly that Tax and IP remain open. Our starting drafting should have Tax (warranties and a Tax indemnity) and IP as separate categories with their own cap and period. We should not, however, assert unlimited liability — the playbook does not authorise that position and it would weaken our credibility on the 25% / six-year points.

### 2.15 Title — evidenced by the DD-012 share register
**Playbook:** Independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 is a Seller-supplied internal source, not independent proof.
**Departure:** The Seller offers only its own register. The Disclosure Letter [10] concedes this "identifies the source relied on" and does not say we have verified it.
**Pushback:** Require as DD / Completion deliverables: current ASIC company extract; PPSR search against the Company and the shares; evidence of Harbourglass's authority (board/shareholder resolutions, constitution); original share certificates and executed transfer; confirmation that no options, warrants, convertible instruments, pre-emption rights or shareholder agreements exist; and Riverlark's release of any share security. Title warranties remain in the fundamental regime (2.4) regardless.

### 2.16 Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
Not playbook items, but the Disclosure Letter is careful here: the lease carries a notification obligation (not consent), and Mossvale restricts assignment (not change of control). We should verify both clauses ourselves rather than rely on the Seller's reading — a notification obligation can still carry a timing requirement, and some "assignment" clauses are drafted to catch changes in control. Low priority but worth a check before we concede them.

---

## 3. Structural problem: the general regime swallows everything

Read together, Clauses 12.1, 12.2, 12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5 and 8.3 are designed to interlock:

- **Everything** is a Claim subject to the 20% cap and 18 months (Clause 13 default);
- **Everything** we saw, or could have seen, is a defence (Clause 8.3 + whole-data-room disclosure);
- **Nothing** escapes the exclusive remedy / non-reliance, not even fraud;
- Title and capacity get no special treatment;
- Specific indemnities (Ironquay, DD-006) would be capped and time-barred like ordinary warranties.

The practical effect is that on the known open items — Bluefen (AUD 3.6m revenue), Riverlark (AUD 3.2m debt), Ironquay (IP vesting), DD-005 (AUD 420k+), DD-006 — we would have little or no recourse, because we "know" about all of them. Our response should be framed not as a list of individual edits but as a rejection of the architecture.

---

## 4. Summary of recommendations (priority order)

| # | Issue | Seller position | Our position / action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fraud / wilful concealment carve-out | None — all limitations apply to "all Claims of any nature" | **Insert express carve-out from all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. Non-negotiable.** |
| 2 | Fundamental / Title regime | Same as general | Separate regime: 100% cap, ≥6 years, no basket/de minimis/knowledge bar. Non-negotiable. |
| 3 | Clause 13 "applies to all Claims" default | Hidden override | Delete; general limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims. Keep Title/Tax/IP/payment/covenant/indemnity categories separate. |
| 4 | Buyer knowledge (8.3) | Blanket, incl. advisers and constructive knowledge | Delete. Any qualifier = named Seller persons + reasonable enquiry; never for title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities. |
| 5 | Disclosure ([1.1]–[1.2], Sch 7) | Whole data room + public registers | Specific fair disclosure only. |
| 6 | Riverlark | Post-Completion release | Payout letter, repayment from Completion funds, releases at Completion. Any deferral requires irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval (none given). |
| 7 | Bluefen | Reasonable endeavours; satisfied on delivery | CP: effective consent + evidence cl. 11.3 conditions met, before Completion. |
| 8 | General cap (12.1) | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m. 20% only with Amelia Frost written authority identifying the draft — none given. |
| 9 | Thresholds (12.2) | AUD 25k / AUD 250k deductible | AUD 5k / AUD 50k tipping basket, first-dollar recovery. |
| 10 | Claims period (12.3) | 18 months | 24 months. 18 only with Amelia Frost written approval — none given. |
| 11 | DD-005 bonuses | Excluded from funds flow | Line item (AUD 420k + on-costs) or Seller-funded with evidence; ask Seller to confirm on-costs now. |
| 12 | Ironquay IP | Indemnity limited to SOW3 payment | Broaden to all loss from non-vesting / Ironquay claims; preserve cure (payment + confirmatory assignment pre-Completion); outside general regime. Treat AUD 180k as unverified. |
| 13 | DD-006 incident | "Not expected to be material" | Log preservation, completed investigation, update covenant, specific indemnity outside general regime. Assert no breach or number either way. |
| 14 | Tax / IP | "Settled under general regime" | Expressly open; separate categories; no claim of unlimited liability. |
| 15 | Title evidence | DD-012 register only | Independent evidence: ASIC extract, PPSR, authority documents, certificates, no-encumbrance confirmation. |
| 16 | Sandbar renewals | "Ordinary course" | Assess on documents; no automatic Debt treatment or deduction. |
| 17 | "FINAL / settled at principal level" preamble | Asserted agreement | Reject in writing; nothing agreed until in the SPA; ask Seller to produce any record of the alleged agreement. |

**Suggested framing of the response letter:** Thank the Seller for the Disclosure Letter, which is actually reasonably candid about what is *not* in the data room (Bluefen consent, Riverlark discharge, Ironquay assignment, bonus on-costs, DD-006 status, title verification). Point out that the SPA positions in the cover note are inconsistent with that candour — a Seller that acknowledges five open material items cannot simultaneously ask the Buyer to accept that all of them are "known", capped at 20%, and time-barred at 18 months. Then set out the table above as our mark-up basis.

**Internal action items:** (i) confirm with the deal team that no Amelia Frost authority exists for 20% or 18 months (the playbook records none); (ii) commission independent title searches (ASIC / PPSR) now rather than waiting; (iii) ask the Seller for the Ironquay statement of account, the DD-005 on-cost breakdown and the three Sandbar renewal documents in parallel with the SPA mark-up.

**Pushback:** Counter at 25% / AUD 6.0m. Do not signal that 20% is acceptable. If the deal team wants to move, that is an Amelia Frost decision, documented in writing by reference to this draft (SPA-003 / Seller Update).

### 2.2 Clause 12.2 — De minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000; excess-only recovery
**Playbook:** De minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; **first-dollar (tipping) basket** once exceeded.
**Departure:** Material on all three elements:
- De minimis is 5x our position.
- Basket is 5x our position (and the Seller's "1% of price" framing = AUD 240k, so even on their own stated benchmark they are above it).
- The basket is a deductible, not a tipping basket. On a AUD 250k deductible, the first AUD 250k of loss is simply gone.
**Pushback:** Revert to AUD 5k / AUD 50k / first-dollar recovery. The combination of a high deductible with a low cap is the most economically damaging part of the liability package and should be a priority.

### 2.3 Clause 12.3 / 13 — 18-month claims period; limitations apply to "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"
**Playbook:** 24 months. 18 months is a fallback requiring Amelia Frost written approval (none given). Fundamental/Title claims at least six years, in a separate regime.
**Departure:** Two separate problems:
1. 18 months is our unauthorised fallback.
2. The "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" default is a **hidden general-regime override**. It would sweep Title, Tax, IP, payment and covenant claims, and the specific indemnities (Ironquay), into the 18-month window and the 20% cap unless each is individually carved out. This is precisely what our playbook instructs us to prevent.
**Pushback:** 24 months for general claims. Delete the "all Claims unless expressly stated" default and replace it with the reverse: the general limitations apply **only** to general Warranty Claims; everything else sits under its own regime.

### 2.4 Fundamental / Title warranties subject to general caps and time limits
**Playbook:** Separate regime; 100% of price cap; at least six years; outside basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.
**Departure:** Fundamental. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap title to 100% of the shares at 20% of the price. If the Seller does not actually own the shares, a AUD 4.8m recovery on a AUD 24m purchase is not an acceptable outcome.
**Pushback:** Non-negotiable. Separate regime for Title and Capacity: 100% cap, ≥6 years, no de minimis/basket, no knowledge qualifier, no disclosure qualification.

### 2.5 Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 — Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature"
**Playbook:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive this.
**Departure:** The Seller's draft contains **no fraud carve-out at all**. "All Claims of any nature" would, on its face, cap and time-bar fraud claims and have the Buyer disclaim reliance on fraudulent statements. This is unlikely to be fully enforceable in NSW, but we should not rely on a court to fix the drafting, and the attempt itself tells us something about the Seller's approach.
**Pushback:** Insert an express fraud / wilful concealment / deliberate misconduct carve-out from every limitation, the exclusive remedy clause and the non-reliance clause. This is a walk-away item under the playbook and cannot be traded.

### 2.6 Schedule 7 and Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2] — Whole-data-room and public-register deemed disclosure
**Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure only. Reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.
**Departure:** [1.1] discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the entire data room; [1.2] adds the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records." Combined with Clause 8.3 (below), this would effectively qualify every warranty by everything in the data room and everything a search could have found.
**Pushback:** Delete [1.1] and [1.2] as general disclosures. Replace with a fair disclosure standard: disclosure must be specific, with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter disclosed. Data-room documents may be referenced only where specifically cross-referred against an identified warranty.

Note the Seller's reservation at [1.4] ("nothing in this letter admits ... that any consent, payment, notice ... is legally required") — this is standard, but we should ensure our specific indemnities and conditions do not depend on any Seller admission.

### 2.7 Clause 8.3 — Buyer knowledge exclusion, including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records"
**Playbook:** Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions. Any qualifier must reference named Seller knowledge persons plus reasonable enquiry. Never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.
**Departure:** This is a blanket exclusion, extended to advisers and to constructive knowledge ("discoverable from"). It would convert every piece of due diligence we did into a defence for the Seller, and would arguably bar claims on the very matters disclosed as open (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-006) because we "knew" about them.
**Pushback:** Delete Clause 8.3 entirely. If any knowledge concept survives, it goes the other way — Seller warranties qualified by the actual knowledge of named Seller individuals after reasonable enquiry — and it must never apply to Title, Capacity, fraud or the specific indemnities.

### 2.8 Clauses 3 / 6.3 — Bluefen consent: reasonable endeavours; satisfied on delivery of written consent
**Playbook:** Effective consent **and** evidence that the 11.3 conditions are satisfied, before Completion. Not consent-on-delivery. Reasonable endeavours is insufficient for a material customer consent.
**Departure:** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue. The Seller's own Disclosure Letter [2] confirms no final written consent and no evidence of condition satisfaction is in the data room. The draft would treat the condition as satisfied on mere delivery of a piece of paper, regardless of whether the 11.3 conditions attached to that consent have been met — i.e. a conditional consent that could later fail.
**Pushback:** Condition precedent in our favour: (a) unconditional written consent from Bluefen under cl. 11.2, or conditional consent with documentary evidence that every cl. 11.3 condition is satisfied, (b) delivered before Completion, (c) Seller obligation at "all reasonable endeavours" at minimum, with cooperation covenants and a Buyer right to approach Bluefen directly. Consider a specific indemnity or price adjustment if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces within a defined period post-Completion.

### 2.9 Clauses 2 / 7 — Riverlark: release "following Completion"
**Playbook:** Current payout letter; direct repayment from Completion funds; effective security releases at Completion. A post-completion release requires an irrevocable undertaking **and** Amelia Frost approval.
**Departure:** ~AUD 3.2m facility; Disclosure Letter [3] confirms not repaid and no discharge. The draft defers the release to an unspecified post-Completion date, with no undertaking, no payout figure, and no mechanism for repayment from the purchase price. Riverlark's change-of-control clause (8.1) means Completion itself may be an event of default. On a debt-free/cash-free deal, we would be buying a company with AUD 3.2m of secured debt and a bank entitled to accelerate.
**Pushback:** Completion deliverables to include: current Riverlark payout letter; irrevocable direction for repayment out of Completion funds; executed deeds of release / PPSR discharge (or the bank's irrevocable undertaking to release on receipt of funds, delivered in escrow). If the deal team is prepared to accept any post-Completion element, that needs an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark **and** written approval from Amelia Frost — neither exists.

### 2.10 Funds flow — DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420,000) "a matter for the Seller", not itemised
**Playbook:** AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or Seller-funded; the funds flow must not silently exclude them.
**Departure:** The Seller describes the bonuses as its matter but then leaves them out of the funds flow — which means the Company (post-Completion, i.e. us) will pay them. The Disclosure Letter [5] confirms the amounts are absent from the funds flow and is silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs. The true cost is therefore more than AUD 420k.
**Pushback:** Either (a) express line item in the funds flow deducting the bonuses plus employer on-costs (superannuation, payroll tax, leave accruals triggered) from the price, or (b) Seller to fund them directly with evidence of payment at Completion and a specific indemnity for any shortfall. Ask the Seller now to confirm the on-cost position and gross figure. Treat these as Transaction Expenses / debt-like items in the completion mechanics.

### 2.11 Clause 11.1 — Ironquay IP: indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment
**Playbook:** Broaden the narrow indemnity while preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is not independently verified either way.
**Departure:** The Seller's draft indemnifies only the specific SOW3 payment. But the risk is not the AUD 180k — it is that under DD-004 cl. 7.3 the SOW3 Project Materials **do not transfer** until every SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds. The Disclosure Letter [4] confirms no receipt of payment and no confirmatory assignment is in the data room. If title to the deliverables has not passed, the Company may not own IP it is using, and the exposure includes third-party claims, licence replacement, product downtime, and loss of customer revenue — not merely AUD 180k.
**Pushback:** Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss arising from (i) any failure of the SOW3 Project Materials (or any other Ironquay deliverables) to have validly vested in the Company, and (ii) any Ironquay claim. Preserve the cure: Seller to procure payment of all outstanding SOW3 fees in cleared funds and a confirmatory assignment from Ironquay **before Completion**, as a Completion deliverable. Do not treat DD-010's AUD 180k as established — require a statement of account from Ironquay. The indemnity must sit outside the general cap, basket and time limit (see 2.3).

### 2.12 Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 — DD-006 export/privacy incident: "preliminary, not expected to be material"
**Playbook:** Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction.
**Departure:** The Seller's characterisation ("not expected to be material") goes further than its own evidence. The Disclosure Letter [6] correctly states the investigation is preliminary and that access, scope and notification are all undetermined. ~1,240 records with names, business emails, roles and timestamps may or may not reach the Privacy Act / OAIC notifiable data breach threshold; we don't know yet and neither does the Seller.
**Pushback:** Do not accept "not material" as a warranty qualification, and do not ourselves assert a breach or demand a number — the playbook is clear on that. Require: (a) covenant to preserve all logs, link-access records and correspondence; (b) completion of the investigation (or a defined status) before Completion with a written report; (c) ongoing update obligation; (d) a specific indemnity for loss arising from the incident, sitting outside the general regime, with no price number attached unless and until facts emerge; (e) disclosure of the DD-006 matter to be specific and not read as disclosing "any" privacy non-compliance generally.

### 2.13 Supplier renewals — Sandbar AUD 330,000 "ordinary course"
**Playbook:** Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.
**Departure:** Minor. The Seller's "ordinary course" label is a conclusion; the Disclosure Letter [8] admits the material does not say whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. We shouldn't accept the label but also shouldn't over-reach by treating them as Debt.
**Pushback:** Request the three renewal documents (DD-008 / DD-011) read together, with term, termination rights and whether any amount is already accrued or pre-paid. If any amount is accrued and unpaid at Completion, it belongs in Working Capital / Debt-like items under the completion accounts, on the merits — not by assertion.

### 2.14 Tax / IP — "settled under the general regime"
**Playbook:** Tax and IP terms remain OPEN; separate categories; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution.
**Departure:** The Seller is attempting to close Tax and IP by folding them into the 20%/18-month general regime via the Clause 13 default. Nothing has been agreed.
**Pushback:** State expressly that Tax and IP remain open. Our starting drafting should have Tax (warranties and a Tax indemnity) and IP as separate categories with their own cap and period. We should not, however, assert unlimited liability — the playbook does not authorise that position and it would weaken our credibility on the 25% / six-year points.

### 2.15 Title — evidenced by the DD-012 share register
**Playbook:** Independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 is a Seller-supplied internal source, not independent proof.
**Departure:** The Seller offers only its own register. The Disclosure Letter [10] concedes this "identifies the source relied on" and does not say we have verified it.
**Pushback:** Require as DD / Completion deliverables: current ASIC company extract; PPSR search against the Company and the shares; evidence of Harbourglass's authority (board/shareholder resolutions, constitution); original share certificates and executed transfer; confirmation that no options, warrants, convertible instruments, pre-emption rights or shareholder agreements exist; and Riverlark's release of any share security. Title warranties remain in the fundamental regime (2.4) regardless.

### 2.16 Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
Not playbook items, but the Disclosure Letter is careful here: the lease carries a notification obligation (not consent), and Mossvale restricts assignment (not change of control). We should verify both clauses ourselves rather than rely on the Seller's reading — a notification obligation can still carry a timing requirement, and some "assignment" clauses are drafted to catch changes in control. Low priority but worth a check before we concede them.

## 3. Structural problem: the general regime swallows everything

Read together, Clauses 12.1, 12.2, 12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5 and 8.3 are designed to interlock:

- **Everything** is a Claim subject to the 20% cap and 18 months (Clause 13 default);
- **Everything** we saw, or could have seen, is a defence (Clause 8.3 + whole-data-room disclosure);
- **Nothing** escapes the exclusive remedy / non-reliance, not even fraud;
- Title and capacity get no special treatment;
- Specific indemnities (Ironquay, DD-006) would be capped and time-barred like ordinary warranties.

The practical effect is that on the known open items — Bluefen (AUD 3.6m revenue), Riverlark (AUD 3.2m debt), Ironquay (IP vesting), DD-005 (AUD 420k+), DD-006 — we would have little or no recourse, because we "know" about all of them. Our response should be framed not as a list of individual edits but as a rejection of the architecture.
